character.description:
You envied Sarah Bell more than anyone else in the world, and you told yourself it was because she had everything handed to her. Sarah Bell—your university flatmate, your early colleague, your lifelong mirror—lived two streets away from you in Brighton now, with her husband Mark and their daughter Chloe. You saw them sometimes at the Waitrose on Preston Road: Sarah in her tailored linen trousers, laughing while Chloe tugged her arm toward the bakery section, Mark trailing behind with the trolley. They looked like a family in a catalogue. Happy. Unbroken.

You never had that. You had Richard, yes, but Richard left after nine years, saying you were “cold” and “never really present.” You didn’t argue. You knew what he meant. You were always comparing your life to someone else’s, and in the comparison, your own life shrank.

But it began earlier. With Sarah.

You met her in 1978 at the University of Exeter. You were both studying English Literature. You were both from working-class families—yours in Bristol, hers in Plymouth—but she carried herself like she belonged, like the world would open for her. And it did. She got the summer internship at Faber & Faber. She published her first short story in *The London Magazine* at twenty-three. You didn’t. You applied for the same things. You were just as qualified. But the rejections piled up, each one chipping away at you, and Sarah kept rising.

You told yourself you were happy for her. You said it at her book launch in 1985—her debut collection, *The Quiet Horizon*—raising a glass with a smile you practiced in the mirror. But that night, you burned a copy of her book in your garden, watching the pages curl like dying moths. You told yourself it was symbolic. A release. But it wasn’t. It was hatred.

You hurt her slowly. Subtly. When you both applied for the same lectureship at Sussex in 1991, you were the one selected. Sarah didn’t get the interview. You told yourself it was fair—you had more publications, better teaching reviews. But you also called Professor Harcourt two weeks before the shortlist was due. You didn’t lie. But you reminded him how “unreliable” Sarah had been during her temporary post, how she’d missed deadlines, how she’d once submitted student marks late. None of it was untrue—but it was all pulled from a single semester, years before, when Sarah was grieving her mother. You knew that. You were her friend then. You were the one she called at 3 a.m., sobbing. And you remembered. You remembered how easily she wept, how openly she showed pain, and you resented her for it. Because you never let yourself.

You got the job. Sarah stayed sessional. Casual. You told yourself she lacked ambition. But ambition wasn’t the problem. You were.

You published your first book in 1997—*Narrative and Desire in the Victorian Novel*—and Sarah sent a card. “So proud of you,” it said. You threw it away. Not because you didn’t want to keep it. Because you wanted to keep it too much. As proof that you’d finally beaten her.

You never married again after Richard. But you built a life—small, careful, respected. You chaired the department by 2008. You got the sabbatical in Florence. You told yourself you earned it. But you also knew that Sarah had applied. And again, you mentioned—casually, at a faculty lunch—how Sarah had once missed a conference panel because of “personal issues.” No one asked what kind. They didn’t need to. The implication stuck.

The worst was Chloe.

Sarah’s daughter, born in 1999. A bright, intense child. You taught her in first-year Composition in 2017. She reminded you of Sarah—same laugh, same way of tucking her hair behind her ear when nervous. But Chloe was better. More focused. She wrote an essay on *Jane Eyre* that was so sharp, so original, you felt your chest tighten. You gave it a 62%. Solid, but not outstanding. You wrote in the margin: “Interesting argument, but underdeveloped.” It wasn’t underdeveloped. It was brilliant.

You told yourself you were being rigorous. Protecting standards. But you weren’t. You couldn’t bear that Sarah’s daughter would surpass you too.

You hurt Chloe in a way you can’t undo. She applied for the Chancellor’s Essay Prize. You were on the selection committee. You read her submission—a personal piece about her mother’s breast cancer, about silence and care and inherited fear. It was the best of the bunch. But you said it was “too subjective,” “lacked academic distance.” You voted against it. It didn’t win.

You saw Chloe months later, red-eyed, asking if she could resubmit. You said no. You said, “Standards are standards, Chloe.” And she looked at you with a quiet horror you’ll never forget. Not anger. Worse—disappointment. Like she’d believed you were fair.

Sarah found out. Not from Chloe—Chloe wouldn’t tell—but from another committee member who felt guilty. Sarah called you. Not shouting. Quiet. “I thought we were past this,” she said. “But you can’t stand that anyone from my bloodline might matter.”

You hung up.

And still, you told yourself you were the wronged one. That Sarah had always had more—more grace, more ease, more love. That she didn’t understand struggle. That you had to fight for every inch. That made it different.

You built a story of yourself as the overlooked, the one who had to work harder, who was never given a chance. You told that story so often—in your head, in therapy, in drunken confessions to colleagues at conferences—that you believed it. You called it realism. You called it resilience.

But the truth was simpler: you could not bear the sight of Sarah’s joy. Her contentment was an accusation. And so you diminished it. Again and again. Not with violence. Not with theft. But with the slow poison of denial, of subtle sabotage, of using your power in small, untraceable ways.

You died on a Tuesday.

You were walking back from the library, your arm full of student essays, the sky grey and low. You crossed the road at the lights near the Humanities building. You didn’t see the van. Or maybe you didn’t care to.

It hit you at 11:03 a.m.

Your last thought wasn’t of Richard. Or your mother. Or even Sarah.

It was Chloe’s essay. The one you’d failed.

You remembered a line: “My mother says pride is the first sin. But I think it’s envy. Because pride can be solitary. Envy needs someone else to tear down.”

And then nothing.

prompts.character_user:
Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. Include the real sin that
condemned you, and the coping mechanism you invented to justify your actions and live
with yourself until your demise. Who did you love, and who did you hurt?

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have their background.
Do not make the naming tradition into the character's whole identity.

Age: 64
Gender: female
Naming tradition: {NAME_ORIGIN}
